newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: INTERVIEW-CMG sees continued strong growth.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-CMG sees continued strong growth.

text.p: Anglo-Dutch information technology company CMG Plc is confident it can keep beating market growth rates of 10-15 percent as demand for its services continues to surge in the run up to the new millennium.

"If you look at the computer software services marketplace now we believe it's growing at the moment at between 10 and 15 percent, probably more towards the 15," CMG chairman Cor Stutterhiem said in an interview on Monday.
Last year CMG's turnover increased by some 25 percent as it forged ahead in Europe's buoyant IT markets.
"The growth of towards the 15 percent probably started last year and certainly this year. We expect this growth of between 10 and 15 to continue past the year 2000," said Stutterheim.

"We will do better than that. I can say that with justification because we have been doing that," he said. "Do I expect it to carry on? It's going to be another good year. I expect to outperform the market averages."

He said 1996's 25 percent turnover growth, to 245 million stg, was achieved against the background of a strong pound, demonstrating the underlying strength of a business which generates some 70 percent of its turnover in the Netherlands.
Business at CMG has boomed in the 1990s as IT applications in business have exploded, particularly in the fields of finance and telecommunications.
CMG has seen its turnover balloon from 129 million stg in 1993 and its pre-tax profit soar from 11 million stg in 1993 to 27.5 million in 1996.

"The driving forces (in the IT market) are the need to communicate, the globalisation of business -- 24 hours a day, open seven days a week. Finance for instance, which is a third of our turnover, is globalising," Stutterheim said.

The introduction in 1999 of a new single European currency, the euro, and the huge task of protecting computer systems from technical, systems dating problems caused by the advent of a new millennium, are seen as big money spinners for CMG.
Many companies are expected to use the enforced changes brought about by the euro and millennium problem to overhaul and replace systems, generating even more revenue for CMG.
"Converting a system to a euro-accepting system may cost 10 million and a new system would be 12 million so why not upgrade? Companies are spending more money on IT than ever," he said.
Stutterheim said potential problems with the euro and millennium bomb were not yet being taken seriously enough, which could prompt stopgap measures, ironically generating even more business for CMG.

"What will happen in 1998, 1999 is that people are going to put plasters on things, they're going to find emergency ways of doing things and then the emergency things will cause even bigger problems after the year 2000," he said.
But CMG is not just pinning its hopes on those two projects. The internet and its various corporate spinoffs, as well as telecommunications software are seen as rich seams to mine.
"There is an enormous amount of work going on. IT is an art and a profession that says you have to invest or you don't survive," said Stutterheim.
